There were no "neighboring tribes" on the scale of the western civilization. Mesoamerican culture was relatively homogeneous and conservative. Geography insured that. While there was most probably violence during the decline, we don't see warfare in the western sense. Their idea of warfare was much more about prestige than killing. Evidence suggests it was mainly a prolonged drought that lead to city collapse. The milpa output dropped near large scale settlements and instead of sending people into the nearby fields, they built temples and prayed for rain. When prayer failed, people left the cities and the number of small, outlying settlements sharply increased. They did not have roads as we think of them and no pack animals so moving food across large distances was very difficult. Moving into small settlements located where rivers still flowed allowed for more labor aimed at agricultural. The food output almost immediately stabilized. The output of their growing system was staggering and the jungle is highly productive in meat and gatherable resources. No indications of massive population decline. Eventually they built back up with a slightly different style we (modern archeologists) gave the civilization a new name. Then another drought and another decline. The language changes a little bit but not so much that we couldn't decipher it. Modern mayan was the basis for deciphering the writing for all the mesoamerican cultures. There are very interesting exceptions to this cycle. The Toltec's built an empire based on commerce via river travel (huge canoes) and their decline was more of a replacement by submission.
